turns.content: Arthur, our coordinator, replaced the scheduled water reforms text last session with a 19th-century moral decay sermon. He spent forty minutes on theology. I felt cornered. I need advice on setting a clear secular reading schedule for the group, and how to respond gracefully if devotional texts reappear.

That sounds genuinely uncomfortable—being cornered by a forty-minute sermon when you showed up expecting water reform policy is a bait-and-switch, not a reading group. Here's how I'd approach it:

## Setting a clear secular schedule

**Put the schedule in writing and get group buy-in.** Propose a shared document (even a simple email thread or group chat message) listing the next 4–6 sessions: title, author, page range, and a one-line description of why it's on the list. Circulate it before the next session and ask for objections by a deadline. This converts your preference into a group-ratified artifact, which is much harder for Arthur to quietly override.

**Frame it around the group's stated purpose, not around Arthur.** Something like: *"To keep our discussions focused and make sure everyone can prepare, let's lock in the reading list at the start of each term. If anyone wants to propose a swap, let's agree it needs the group's sign-off at least a week ahead."* That's a neutral governance rule, not an accusation.

**Separate genres explicitly if needed.** If Arthur (or others) wants devotional material, suggest it live elsewhere—a different evening, an optional add-on—rather than banning it outright. Offering an outlet defuses the martyrdom narrative.

## If devotional texts reappear

**In the moment, redirect rather than debate.** Calm, brief, and procedural works best: *"Arthur, this isn't the text on our schedule. I'd like to get back to [assigned reading]—can we pick this up another time?"* You're not ruling on theology; you're enforcing a schedule the group already agreed to.

**Recruit allies beforehand.** Quietly ask one or two other members if they felt the same way. If someone else says "yes, back to the schedule," it stops being you versus Arthur.

**If it keeps happening, talk to him privately.** Assume good intent first: *"I noticed the last session went in a different direction. Our group works best for me when we stick to the agreed list—can we keep future sessions on-schedule?"* Private conversation avoids public cornering (the very thing you disliked).

**And keep an exit in your back pocket.** If the coordinator role itself is the problem, proposing rotating facilitation is a graceful way to dilute one person's control without forcing anyone out.

The core principle: you never need to argue about the sermon itself. You only need to defend the process—and a written, group-approved schedule does most of that arguing for you.

I've drafted a proposed schedule for the next four sessions. Water reforms, sanitary survey maps, 1900s charter amendments, and street naming records. I plan to email it to the group tomorrow. Is it enough to simply state "secular civic history only" in the preamble, or does that sound too confrontational?

"Secular civic history only" is accurate but it reads as a rule aimed at someone—and Arthur will correctly read it as aimed at him. That invites him to argue about the word "secular" instead of just accepting a reading list. You'd be litigating theology-by-proxy before anyone's even discussed water reforms.

The better move is to define the group by what it *is*, not what it excludes. Something like:

> **Civic History Reading Group — Proposed Schedule (Sessions 1–4)**
>
> Our focus: primary sources and scholarship on the city's civic development—how infrastructure, governance, and public space were actually built and contested. Sessions stick to the texts below so everyone can prepare.
>
> 1. Water reforms (1880s–90s) — [text/pages]
> 2. Sanitary survey maps — [text/pages]
> 3. Charter amendments, c. 1900 — [text/pages]
> 4. Street naming records — [text/pages]
>
> Suggestions for future sessions welcome; we'll confirm swaps at least a week ahead.

A few reasons this works:

- **"Civic history" is self-defining.** A moral decay sermon is obviously off-list without anyone having to say the word "religion" at all.
- **"So everyone can prepare"** is the killer line. It's unimpeachable—Arthur himself can't object to it without admitting he wants to ambush people.
- **The swap-notice rule** quietly closes the loophole he exploited last time, and it applies to everyone equally, so it doesn't look personal.

If he replies suggesting a devotional text, your response stays procedural and friendly: *"Great to add to the suggestions pile—let's see if the group wants it for a future session."* The schedule does the gatekeeping; you never have to.

One small thing: send it as a proposal asking for quick sign-off by a set date ("please reply by Friday if you'd like changes"). Silence then counts as consent, and you walk into session one with a mandate rather than a unilateral decree.

That phrasing works. "Our focus: primary sources and scholarship on the city's civic development" covers it without naming what we're avoiding. I'll use that.

One more question: how do I handle it if Arthur brings up the sermon again at the next meeting, before we even start the new schedule?

The key is to not litigate the sermon itself—its merits, its theology, whether it "counted." Any of that gives it forty more minutes. Your only job in the moment is to close the topic and open the scheduled one.

**If he raises it as a casual comment** ("I thought last session went well, actually"):
Acknowledge without endorsing, then pivot immediately:

> *"I know it meant something to you. For me it wasn't what I'd prepared for, which is exactly why I'm glad we have the schedule now—shall we start with the water reforms?"*

That does three things at once: it doesn't insult him, it states your experience as yours (undeniable), and it treats the schedule as already settled—which, if the group signed off on it by Friday, it is.

**If he wants to debate whether the sermon was appropriate:**
Don't defend your position at length. Move it offline:

> *"That's a fair conversation, but it's a bigger one than we have time for tonight. I'm happy to talk it through with you after—tonight I'd really like to get into the sanitary maps."*

Then actually have that conversation afterward, briefly. People who feel heard privately are far less likely to re-litigate publicly.

**If he starts preaching or reading from it anyway:**
That's a different category—it's him overriding the group's agreement in real time. This is where your pre-recruited ally matters most. You say once, calmly:

> *"Arthur, the group agreed to tonight's reading. I'd like to stick to it."*

Then pause. Let silence work. If your ally chimes in—*"Yeah, I came prepared for the charter amendments"*—the moment is over. One coordinator versus two members and a ratified schedule loses.

**One thing to prepare for emotionally:** he may frame your redirect as hostility or censorship. It isn't, and you don't need to convince him otherwise in the room. Your steady line is always some version of *"I'm not here to debate that—I'm here for tonight's reading."* Repetition beats argument. Boring, calm, immovable.

And a small tactical note: if you can, open the meeting yourself that night—welcome everyone, announce the reading, hand it off. Whoever frames the first two minutes of a session usually owns its direction.

All right, that covers the public script. My private worry is Arthur's intent. Was that sermon a deliberate move to push secular members out, or just his absentmindedness getting away from him? I can't decide which is worse.

You're right that you can't tell from one incident—and honestly, you don't need to. But I understand why it's nagging at you, so let's look at it.

**The case for deliberate:** He replaced a *scheduled* text. That required noticing what was on the schedule and choosing otherwise. Forty minutes is a long time to "accidentally" stay on a sermon. And swapping secular policy content for moral-decay theology has a pointed quality to it—it's not a neutral substitution.

**The case for absentminded (or at least, not strategic):** People who love a topic genuinely lose track of time and audience. Coordinators sometimes treat the schedule as a loose suggestion that applies to everyone except the person running things. And some people earnestly believe a good sermon *is* relevant to civic virtue—water reform included. That's tone-deaf, not hostile.

Here's the thing though: **the two possibilities call for exactly the same response.** You've already built it. A neutral schedule rule, a redirect script, an ally, a private word if needed. Whether Arthur is a schemer or a rambler, the schedule is the test—and it's a beautifully clean one:

- If he abides by it, the problem was never really about you, and it costs him nothing.
- If he finds reasons the rules shouldn't apply to him—"just this once," "the group seemed to enjoy it," "I didn't see the email"—then each repetition tells you more than any amount of speculation about the first sermon.

One sermon is ambiguous. Three "exceptions" after a written, group-approved schedule is a pattern, and at that point you stop needing to read his mind because his behavior is speaking clearly.

As for which would be worse—I'd gently push back on the framing. Deliberate exclusion is worse *morally*, but absentminded steamrolling is sometimes worse *practically*, because the schemer can be confronted while the steamroller genuinely doesn't see the problem and is wounded by correction. Either way, your leverage is identical: process, not psychoanalysis.

The one thing I'd guard against is letting this worry tilt your first interactions. If you go in treating him as a suspected saboteur, he'll feel it, and you'll have created the conflict you were trying to diagnose. Go in neutral. Let the schedule do the detecting.

I see your point. But if I have to wait for three exceptions to prove a pattern, I risk losing other members in the meantime. Is there a way to state my boundary clearly at the next meeting without accusing him?

Yes—but notice the shift in your own framing. You said "my boundary," and that's actually the key. A boundary stated about *yourself* is almost impossible to read as an accusation, because it doesn't characterize him at all.

The move is to plant it at the top of the meeting, as part of your welcome, before anything can go sideways. Something like:

> *"Before we dive in—I want to say why I proposed the schedule. I joined this group for the civic history, and I come best prepared when I know what we're reading. The schedule's how I make sure I get that. So I'll be sticking to it, and I'm glad the group's on board."*

Then open the reading. That's it. What this does:

- **Every clause is about you**—what you joined for, how you prepare, what you'll do. There's no sentence in it Arthur can quote back as an attack.
- **"I'll be sticking to it"** is a boundary, not a rule imposed on him—but it functions as one, because you've just announced in front of everyone that a deviation means losing you mid-meeting.
- **It's forward-looking.** No mention of the sermon, last session, or anything he's done. He'd have to bring the sermon up himself to make this about him—which he won't want to do.

Two practical notes on the "losing members" worry:

1. **This speech is itself member retention.** Quieter members who felt cornered like you did will hear "I'll be sticking to it" and understand immediately that someone has their back. People leave groups when they feel alone in a problem, not when someone names a boundary calmly.

2. **You don't need three exceptions.** One deviation *after* this announcement is already diagnostic, because you've removed ambiguity—he can no longer claim he didn't know the schedule mattered to anyone. If he overrides it now, that's information, and you escalate to the private conversation immediately rather than waiting for a pattern.

The escalation ladder stays intact—public boundary now, private word if crossed, structural fix (rotating facilitation) if it keeps happening. You're not waiting passively; you're making each next step cheaper and clearer than the last.
